interactions.summary: A cynical aside suggests denial, another student distinguishes human trust from divine judgment, Jiang demands a concrete path of redemption, and the answer that emerges is slow character change proven over time by not repeating the betrayal.

Jiang then shifts the discussion deeper by asking why cheating is bad at all, drawing one student's attempt to minimize a one-off lapse and another student's answer that genuine remorse visible to the other partner is the only real basis for restoration.

speaker_notes.note: This short line is best read as a cynical joke rather than a serious proposed solution.

claims.claim: A student distinguishes God from human spouses by arguing that human reconciliation is about regaining trust, whereas God does not face the same problem of trust or wounded judgment.
The class's concrete answer to Jiang is that redemption would mean a changed character sustained over time, shown by not cheating again because one cannot go back and undo the original act.
claims.temporal_scope: Student answer under Jiang's questioning on 2026-06-15.

claims.claim: Jiang refuses to let the class stop at repair-techniques and instead asks for the underlying moral logic of why cheating counts as a serious wrong in the first place.

One student tries to soften the offense by treating a one-time affair as a mistake rather than a true relationship, while another says the only path back is for the betrayed partner to see genuine remorse.

signature_moments.moment: The packet's cleanest formulation of irreversible guilt is the claim that you cannot go back in time and un-cheat; all you can do is become a different person.
signature_moments.source_phrase: you can't go back in time and not an un-cheat
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It condenses the class's whole effort to imagine redemption without magical erasure of the past.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang strips away sentimental consensus by asking who cares about a random one-night affair and forcing the class to articulate the deeper moral structure they are assuming.
signature_moments.source_phrase: Who cares? What, what does it matter?
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It shows Jiang refusing generic moralism and demanding a first-principles account of betrayal.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The human, non-divine frame for redemption as rebuilding another person's confidence through long character change.
A student's phrase for the visible remorse that might let the betrayed partner see moral seriousness rather than indifference.

chronology_notes.note: This June 15 packet deepens the redemption discussion from outward forgiveness to irreversibility, changed character, regained trust, and the need to explain why betrayal is morally corrosive at all.

uncertainty_notes.note: The Clinton example is ASR-rough, but the student's point is clear: she is trying to downgrade a one-time affair from deep betrayal to forgivable mistake.
